extracted.intended_audience: university trustees, faculty, practicing scientists, and field ethnographers
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive guidance on (1) methods for appointing university teachers and organizing initial faculties, and (2) proper scientific and ethnographic methods — emphasizing experiment over anatomy and immersive fieldwork for studying mythology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of personal acquaintance in recommendations
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommendors who know the aspirant personally (long personal acquaintance) provide information 'worth much more than any information derived from mere formal letters of recommendation or from hearsay.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personal knowledge of a candidate's past work and probable capabilities produces safer appointments and candidates likely to work in harmony with colleagues; such recommendations are preferred over formal letters or hearsay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faculty unanimous recommendation as basis for appointment
rubrics_metrics.description: At institutions with an existing faculty, appointments should be made upon the unanimous recommendation of the faculty (example: Sheffield Scientific School).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When faculty recommend a candidate unanimously, trustees and appointing bodies will be gratified and the appointee will be likely to accept; reliance on faculty consensus fosters a harmonious, efficient, and strong school.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure for appointments in newly organized schools
rubrics_metrics.description: For schools in process of organization, trustees should select a strong and competent president in whom they have full confidence and give him almost autocratic powers to choose the first faculty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let the chosen president draw around him teachers who will work in unison; once the initial faculty is formed, refer subsequent appointments to that body. Trustees should not surrender their authority, but should generally respect faculty recommendations except for the most substantial reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appointments method should be policy-driven, not rigid rule
rubrics_metrics.description: The method by which teachers are appointed should be a matter of usage and policy, not of prescribed rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flexible, experience-based policies (grounded in usage) better ensure harmonious faculty functioning than overly rigid prescriptions; distrust between trustees and faculty leads to mischief and harm to students.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faculty harmony as a criterion of institutional efficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: A faculty cannot maintain the highest efficiency unless it is thoroughly harmonious; any jar or friction leads to dissatisfactions which spread to students and are disastrous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selection and appointment practices should aim to create a harmonious body of teachers; methods that secure mutual confidence and compatibility are preferred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimentation over anatomy for physiological discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: Anatomy alone is insufficient for the advancement of physiological science; experiment is necessary to establish functional doctrines (e.g., motor vs sensory nerve-roots).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples (Bell, Walker, Magendie, Müller) show that anatomical preconceptions misled investigators and that carefully devised experiments ultimately established correct physiological doctrine. Do not treat anatomical inference as conclusive without experimental confirmation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design experiments carefully and use appropriate models
rubrics_metrics.description: Experimental conclusions require carefully devised methods and, where necessary, extension across models (e.g., Müller's frog experiments then extended to warm-blooded animals) to resolve ambiguities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apparent paradoxes (e.g., irritation of different roots producing pain or movement) may be resolved by experimental designs that trace reflex circuits and separate direct from indirect effects. Rigorous, reproducible methods are essential for conclusive results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be open to correction and properly acknowledge others' experimental contributions
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientists should accept and acknowledge corrections supplied by others' experiments rather than appropriating corrections without attribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text criticizes Bell for adopting corrections made by Magendie (and others) without clear acknowledgment; ethical scientific conduct requires transparency about sources and changes to prior accounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overconfidence in limited knowledge ('a little knowledge' warning)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'A little knowledge is dangerous' when it leads its possessor to imagine that he or she knows all about the subject; teaching limited knowledge as whole truth is doubly dangerous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students and teachers should recognize the provisional nature of partial understanding and not present incomplete results as final; this applies to historical interpretation and scientific claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethnographic immersion and rapport-building for studying mythology
rubrics_metrics.description: To comprehend a people's mythology, one must learn their language, acquire their confidence, assimilate by joining in everyday and religious life, participate as far as possible, and 'strike every possible chord of human sympathy' in intercourse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective ethnographic study requires deep immersion: linguistic competence, participation in social and religious practices, reciprocal trust, and empathetic engagement (even to the point of adopting modes of thought analogous to childhood reasonings) to be an imperfect but credible exponent of the group's beliefs.
